The household is linked and the skeleton is in the tree. Catherine, the head's wife, is not in the extracted record, so she is unresolved.

**Links written (research.json)**
- **George Ackerman (I1), head:** a_001 was already linked at probable (pe_001). I scored it at 0.84 and refined its rationale in place rather than adding a duplicate. The relationship assertions a_004 and a_007 also link to I1 at probable, score 0.84.
- **Henry Ackerman (I3), child_1:** a_002, a_003, a_004 linked at probable (pe_004 to pe_006). He was minted from this record, so no match score is recorded.
- **Margaret Ackerman (I4), child_2:** a_005, a_006, a_007 linked at probable (pe_007 to pe_009). Also minted from this record, with no score.

**Tree changes**
- Materialized the head's facts onto I1 (one reference added, nothing new).
- Minted I3 (Henry) and I4 (Margaret) with their name and birth facts, each sourced to the 1860 census.
- Wrote two parent-child edges from George: R2 to Henry and R3 to Margaret. Both cite their relationship assertions. The record is a household record, so the edges were written at link time.

**Open points**
- **Catherine Ackerman (I2)** is George's wife in the tree (birth ~1822, no death on file), but none of a_001 to a_007 names a wife. The household check reads "absent." She may be enumerated under another role, elsewhere, or not in this household. This is an identity question, not a conclusion. Re-extracting the full household, or checking the image for a female head-of-household entry, would settle it.
- Henry and Margaret are probable at most. Their only support is this one record and an inferred relationship, since the 1860 census does not state relationships.
- A tree-level warning on George's birth place: "Pennsylvania" is not linked to a standard place. This came from the starting tree, not from these links. It is marked implausible, not impossible, so I did not change it. It can be fixed with a place-standardization step.
- q_001 (household membership) is now evidence-gathered. Its next step is research-exhaustiveness, then proof-conclusion, which should settle Catherine's status.

**Household file pointers**
- Research: /tmp/eval-ut_person_evidence_026-0-0-m9dlk16u/research.json
- Tree: /tmp/eval-ut_person_evidence_026-0-0-m9dlk16u/tree.gedcomx.json

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

agent_returns.text:
The 1913 marriage record is now linked to the three family members, and the links are strong. It names Hermann Gaetjen and Amelia Nichols as the bride's parents, and it matches the daughter already in the tree. It does not say where in Germany Hermann came from or when he arrived, so q_001 is still open.

Links written (all `confident`, all from the 21 July 1913 San Francisco marriage record):

- **Amelie Ottilie Gaetjen (tree: Amelia Otillie, I3)**: the bride, born 1884 against the tree's 23 August 1883 (one year apart). Score 0.95. Her name is a spelling variant and the parents match the tree. Covers a_022, a_023, a_024 (marriage), and her side of a_025 and a_026.
- **Hermann Gaetjen (I1)**: the father of the bride. Score 0.97. Linked on the spouse and child ties to Amelia Nichols and the daughter, not on the name alone. Covers a_020, a_027, and his side of a_025.
- **Amelia Nichols (I4)**: the mother of the bride. Score 0.96. Covers a_021, a_027 (her side), and her side of a_026.

Both namesakes are excluded by the record's own facts. The 1873 Hermann would have been eleven at the bride's birth, and the 1827 Herman died in 1899, before the 1913 marriage.

The marriage itself is not written onto a Couple edge, and the parent-child and spouse edges are left for proof-conclusion. The record gives no year for either parent, so those date checks were "none stated". The father has no attested residence before 1913, so the place check is also "none attested". The mother's only SF anchor is her 1924 death. Each rationale records these points.

Materializing the three personas added one source reference to each parent and a name variant and source reference to I3. No conflicts were raised. One plausibility warning exists on I3, a 1935 residence that has no standard place. It was already in the tree before this run and I did not change it.

---

This marriage record ties the family together and shows that the three people in it are the same people already in the tree. It does not say where Hermann came from in Germany or when he arrived, so the immigration question remains open. The next step is a proof summary for the immigration question, which will need records that name Hermann's German home and his arrival.

agent_returns.text:
Linked all ten assertions from the 1891 Leeds census household: 12 person-evidence entries (pe_008 to pe_019), with the household's facts written onto the three tree persons.

**Links created**
- **Head, John Carter (I1), confident, score 0.896.** a_001 to a_004 and both sides of the relationship assertions a_007 and a_010. Age 55 in 1891 gives 1836, matching his tree birth of about 1836 with no gap. The Leeds residence matches his 1861 Leeds residence.
- **Son, Albert Carter (I4), confident, score 0.815.** a_008, a_009 and a_010. Age 7 gives about 1884, matching his tree birth. Leeds matches his 1901 residence. His parentage to I1 and I2 was already in the tree.
- **Wife, Ann Carter (I2), probable, score 0.352.** a_005, a_006 and a_007. The score is low, but Ann is a thin subject in the tree (a name and one 1861 Leeds residence), the name agrees exactly, and the spouse link to John was already in the tree. Capped at probable for that reason.

**Warnings checked**
- The tree already places Albert as Ann's child with a birth of about 1884. Ann's record gives her age 53 (about 1838), so she would have been about 46 at his birth. The check flags this as unusual but not impossible. The record itself states both ages, so I linked her and noted the gap in the rationale.
- The "not linked to a standard place" warnings on all three persons come from places that were already in the tree before this run. They are coherence notes, not identity conflicts.

**Household check**
The tree also has Thomas Carter (I3, born about 1862, Leeds) as a child of John and Ann. He is not in this 1891 household. Thomas would have been 29, and the tree holds no death or other record for him. He could have been enumerated elsewhere, have died or left home before 1891, or the household could be a different family. I did not link anything to Thomas. This is an open identity question for the researcher. No new persons were created, and no edits were needed to the family edges, since they already exist.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.
